tips.title: Build the pyramid — and earn the peak
tips.insight: Base = easy running + steady aerobic. Middle = threshold (LT1/LT2). Peak = VO2/aerobic power + race-specific work. You cannot add the peak without the middle: 'you have to earn the peak'. But once you push the peak, everything below it improves with it — threshold gets faster, easy-run HR drops.
tips.apply: Your plan phases follow this: Base builds the bottom, Build adds threshold, Peak adds VO2 + marathon-specific work. Don't skip ahead to hard intervals in Base.

tips.title: The correlation chain: VO2 → aerobic power → LT2 → race pace
tips.insight: 'If your VO2 isn't where it needs to be, your LT2 is not going to get to where it needs to be. There's always a correlation.' Work backwards from the goal: race pace needs LT2 ~10-15s/km faster, which needs aerobic power faster again, which needs VO2 faster again.
tips.apply: For a 3:30 marathon (4:58/km): LT2 must reach ~4:45-4:50/km, VO2 reps ~4:15-4:25/km. That's the chain your zones are being pulled toward. Today's chain says ~3:45-3:50 — the gap is the training.

tips.title: Steady aerobic days, not zone-2 dogma
tips.insight: 'Whenever I've raced well, there's been plenty of work at steady aerobic.' 2-3 runs per week, roughly 25-30% of weekly volume, ~30s/km slower than threshold. The mindset is the point: 'I've decided I'm going to work today' — not a jog. Pace is the priority; physiology follows.
tips.apply: Your Thursday steady run is exactly this. Treat it as a work day: get the sweat going, no stopping, hold the pace.

tips.title: The luxury run
tips.insight: Zone 1 easy jogs: 'Doesn't matter what the pace is, doesn't matter what the pulse is. It's a luxury run. I don't think I'm building fitness, I'm spending time running — and a lot of runners could get a lot better by just spending time running.'
tips.apply: Easy days after hard days: zero pressure. If in doubt, slower. These runs buy you the volume that makes everything else work.

tips.title: Threshold every 3-4 days, and track it weekly
tips.insight: 'Once every 3-4 days make sure you're doing some LT1 or LT2. Build that middle bit of your pyramid, make it beefy.' Formats are simple: 3×15min at the bottom of threshold, 3×10min or 30min straight at the top end. 'Keep threshold where it needs to be. Track that weekly. Don't let it slip.'
tips.apply: Your Tuesday quality slot rotates through these. The real test of threshold: it should FEEL sustainable for 50-70 minutes. If a 'threshold' rep cooks you, it was too fast.

tips.title: Touch VO2 at least every 10 days or it decays
tips.insight: 'If I leave it two weeks without training above threshold, it feels harder and it's slower.' Vary the stimulus: 5-6×1k, 15×1min, 10×60s uphill, or a 5k time trial. A time trial has a bonus: 'if you're willing to do a 5k time trial, everything else starts to feel easier — no reps can hurt you after that.'
tips.apply: In Build/Peak phases your VO2 day covers this. Every ~6 weeks, swap it for a 5K time trial — it recalibrates all your zones AND toughens you.

tips.title: Become a diesel engine
tips.insight: The body stores only ~100 minutes of threshold-intensity fuel, but your race lasts 3:30+. So the marathon is raced at LT1, not LT2 — and normal training never exposes a weak LT1. 'You don't find out until race day that your LT1 isn't in a great place.'
tips.apply: This is why your plan has so much easy/steady/long running and why the long run stays controlled. You're building fuel efficiency, not just speed.

tips.title: The HR drift test — your monthly check
tips.insight: On a steady or long run, let HR stabilise over the first 5k (say 140-145). Over the next 15-20k at the SAME pace, drift should be max 8-10 beats. A 15-20 beat drift = LT1 weak. Improvement looks like: same pace, average HR down ~5 beats month over month, and max HR down too.
tips.apply: Your Warsaw 15k (HR 156 avg) is the baseline. Re-run that test monthly at fixed pace ~6:00/km — the app's session scores will show the HR trend.

tips.title: Keep the long run boring — sexy stuff trains the wrong engine
tips.insight: 'You can throw intervals in — bloody good long run, but you trained the wrong bloody energy system.' Pushing tempo inside an aerobic long run teaches the body to burn MORE carbs, the opposite of marathon fuel efficiency. Keep pulse 5-10+ beats below marathon HR; at most, progress the last 5-8k slightly.
tips.apply: Your Sunday long runs: flat effort, Z2 HR, accept the boredom. MP segments only appear in the Peak phase, where they belong. Seek company if it stops you racing the long run.

tips.title: Long run every 7-10 days, built patiently
tips.insight: Once a week, or every 10 days if injury-prone. Build duration first (80-90 min, then more) at an unremarkable pace — 'this isn't a marathon run yet, it's just a run. There's nothing sexy about this yet.'
tips.apply: Your 120-minute Sunday runs at 6:00/km are exactly the right kind of boring. The plan grows them toward 30-32k.

tips.title: Alternating tempo — pulls LT1 up to LT2
tips.insight: From 10-12 weeks out (practice earlier every 10-14 days): 1k at LT2 / 1k float at marathon pace +10-15s. Start at 16k total, grow to 20k, then 6×2k with 1k float, then 5×3k. The LT2 km should feel 'a decent effort', never killing. It teaches lactate clearing and fuel efficiency at speed.
tips.apply: This is your Thursday session in the Peak phase. The float is the secret — don't jog it, hold MP+10-15s.

tips.title: The last 4-6 weeks must look like the goal
tips.insight: 'If in the last four to five weeks before a race your training doesn't look like the kind of athlete that's going to achieve the goal, it's very unlikely you'll achieve it.' He audits: how many km at goal race pace in the last 8-10 weeks? Zero km at race pace = don't expect it on race day.
tips.apply: Before your marathon, the app's Race tab compares your recent paces to the goal. If MP km aren't in the log by Peak phase, the goal gets adjusted — that's the deal.

tips.title: ≥10k per week at race pace in the final 5-6 weeks
tips.insight: For a goal half he wants ~10k/week at race-adjacent pace. Can't hold 3k reps at that pace? 'Scale it right back to 1K — but try a 2K rep first.' Manipulate rep length and recovery so pace is achievable.
tips.apply: Peak phase: your MP work (alternating tempo + MP finishes in long runs) sums to 10k+/week at 4:58-5:10. If a rep length breaks you, shorten the rep, not the pace.

tips.title: 60-70% science, 20-30% just work
tips.insight: 'Follow the science for 60-70% — run at that LT2 heart rate. But 20-30% of running comes down to just hard work.' Late in a session (last 2 of 5×2k), forget heart rate and run goal pace, even 10-15s/km faster than HR says. 'You earn that privilege by doing the foundation stuff first.'
tips.apply: In Base: 100% discipline. From Build onward: finish the last reps of quality sessions at goal pace, HR ignored. Never do this in week 1 of a phase.

tips.title: Threshold moves ~5s/km per block — plan for it
tips.insight: Moving threshold 5s/km in a training block is 'awesome, super achievable'. ~10s/km in a year from running alone. The rest comes from other angles: gym, physio, losing a few kg, shoe choice — 'seconds that don't require the fitness to be better'.
tips.apply: Sub-4 needs ~threshold 5:20 (you're near). 3:30 needs ~4:45 — that's a year of blocks, plus the gym you're already doing. This is why we train for 3:30 but bank 3:45.

tips.title: Progress is stepwise — expect a bad race
tips.insight: 'You don't really go from 2:57 to 2:45. You run 2:57, then maybe 3:00, then 2:55, then hover at 2:52.' Improvement across marathons comes in steps with setbacks, 4-5 months apart. Amateurs shouldn't copy elite training — the amateur's mountain is sub-hard aerobic efficiency work at 'a really annoying intensity that is just below hard'.
tips.apply: If a race or test goes badly, it's a data point, not a verdict. The annoying just-below-hard intensity is your steady runs — respect them.

tips.title: Volume protects fitness — and fitness falls as fast as it climbs
tips.insight: 'Once you build fitness to a good place, you've got to protect it. The easiest way is to get out there and do a bit more — even an evening 5k, even a bike ride or rowing. You almost get tired but you get faster.' Track time-per-week and find the number where you're 'firing' — cross-training minutes count.
tips.apply: Your gym days and any cycling count toward weekly load. When fit later in the plan, short second runs or an easy spin protect what you built. The 10% weekly ramp rule is a guideline, not law — but respect tired legs.

tips.title: Tightness means gym, not stretching
tips.insight: 'You think that tightness means you have to stretch. It's got nothing to do with flexibility — you're breaking the muscles down and they're not strong enough.' The fix is the boring basics: calf raises, glute bridges, clams, adductor squeezes, hip control. Plus deliberate carbs and hydration as volume rises.
tips.apply: Your 3 gym days already carry this. Add the boring basics as finishers on every gym day — calves and adductors especially, they're cheap injury insurance.

tips.topic: What a good week looks like
tips.title: His 2:09 week, by zone minutes
tips.insight: Zone 1: ~1.5h. Zone 2: 3-4h. Zone 3 (steady): ~2h. Zone 4 (threshold): 30-35 min. Zone 5: 5-6 min. The middle is beefy; the top is tiny. Also: the first 4-5 weeks of any program are pure discipline — know why before every session, verify after ('did I run in the zone I was supposed to?').
tips.apply: Scaled to your week that's roughly: most km easy/steady, ~30 min of threshold work, a few minutes of VO2. If your hard days are more than ~20% of weekly time, you're racing your training.

tips.topic: How he structures a marathon build
tips.title: The marathon block is 12-16 weeks, in four phases
tips.insight: Phase 1: pre-training - get durable, push threshold, build the 5K/10K ceiling (length depends on where you're coming from). Phase 2 (4-5 wks): the marathon plan proper - introduce tempo, build the long run, grow the big sessions (4x3k -> 4x4k -> 4x5k, 3x8k, 3x10k). END IT WITH A TEST: a half marathon, 10K or long MP tempo. Phase 3 (4-5 wks): fix what the test exposed, hold the rest with minimum dose (intervals every 2 weeks is enough to keep the peak). Then taper.
tips.apply: Your plan now follows exactly this: Foundation until ~14 weeks out, then Build (ends with a test half), then Specific, then a 3-week taper.

tips.topic: How he structures a marathon build
tips.title: Don't race the training in Phase 3
tips.insight: 'A lot of athletes run their race in the third phase.' If sessions start going better than ever, back off: run the first reps slower and only finish fast - 'all you're doing is saving the big result for race day'. Race result = fitness + preparation + taper, and fitness+preparation matter most.
tips.apply: In your Specific phase, when a session feels amazing, that's the signal to bank it, not to push it. The best day of the block must be 18 April.

tips.title: Long run type 1 & 2: volume first, then the 'solid day'
tips.insight: Build pure volume first (his own 2:09 block started at 15 miles where he was DROPPED, and grew week by week: 15-16-17/18-20). Once volume is there, the long run becomes a 'solid day': warm-up ritual, drinks prepared, race intent, ~20-30s/mile slower than race pace, on an imperfect route, NOT in super shoes - 'why should this day be easy?'
tips.apply: Your Foundation/Build Sundays alternate these two. The route should have hills and corners like Vienna will.

tips.title: Long run type 3 & 4: progressive, and race-pace reps
tips.insight: Type 3: progressive - start ~2 min/mile slower than race pace, step down every 4 miles, finish the last miles AT race pace. Type 4: first half steady, second half race-pace work inside the run (6x1 mile, 4x2 mile with 3 min jog, or a sustained MP block). 'Even if you're not fit enough for it yet - run at race pace, make the reps shorter if you must.'
tips.apply: These appear in your Specific phase Sundays, alternating. They're also how you accumulate your weekly race-pace kilometres.

tips.title: The ugly zone: suffer 3-4 times before race day
tips.insight: '100% fact: most people fail the marathon because they never trained for the distance.' From ~week 6-7 of the block, 3-4 sessions must reach the place where you want to stop - legs heavy, psychology asking to quit at 16 miles with 2 to go. Formats: 3x4mi w/2min rest, 4x3mi, or 5mi easy + 10mi at marathon effort. And don't stare at the watch mid-rep: 'heart rate tells you how to feel'. That's what makes 'just another Sunday' true on race day.
tips.apply: Your Specific phase marks 3-4 days as UGLY ZONE. They are the race rehearsals - fuel them fully, finish them, and remember them at km 32.

tips.title: The nibble strategy - never slam a gel
tips.insight: ~10g of carbs every 10 minutes, starting 10 minutes BEFORE the session, through the warm-up and the whole run. Slamming 25g at once spikes insulin and dumps your glucose. Nothing to eat in the 2h before training (or exercise-induced hypoglycemia hits); if you can't eat 2h before, eat nothing and nibble from 10min out. Electrolytes pre-session must be sugar-free ('if it tastes delicious it's throwing your glucose around').
tips.apply: Every quality and long run day in your calendar now carries fueling steps. Race target: practice up to 60-80g/hour on Sunday runs - the gut is trainable and race day is not the day to find out.

tips.title: When training suddenly feels bad, suspect fuel before fitness
tips.insight: 'A lot of the downs are going to be linked to nutrition, 100%.' The 20-minute post-session window is non-negotiable: real carbs + protein, not a 180-calorie bar after a 1000-calorie session. Fuel even steady Z2 runs (~40-50g/h) when the goal is a physiology stimulus - 'get in and get out with the least cost possible'.
tips.apply: Thursday tired? Check what you ate Tuesday-Wednesday before blaming the plan. Post-run meal within 20 minutes, every time.

tips.title: Every 7-10 days, inject your fitness with something hard
tips.insight: 'When you work pretty hard, you get better.' Formats: 10x400m, 5x3min (the Norwegian classic), 10x2min aerobic power, hill reps, or a 5K time trial. The payback is fast: 'your next threshold is quicker and bloody easier' - hard work recalibrates your perceived effort. Then like pizza dough, settle it back down with 10 days of base.
tips.apply: Foundation phase: a VO2 touch every ~10 days even while base-building, plus a 5K time trial every ~6 weeks that recalibrates your zones.

tips.title: Watch stride length x cadence for hidden fatigue
tips.insight: His athlete's stride length dropped 135cm to ~118cm while cadence rose - the body compensating for neuromuscular fatigue, visible weeks before racing felt bad. 'An even easier fix if you were on top of it three, four weeks ago.'
tips.apply: Your Garmin records stride length and cadence. If stride shortens while cadence climbs at the same pace over 2-3 weeks: cut intensity, add sleep, and see it as fatigue - not lost fitness.

tips.title: Make the hardest mile the easiest - and the 3-4 word test
tips.insight: 'If you can't maintain a three to four word conversation, you're not running a tempo.' Mid-session psychology: instead of bracing for mile 3 being hard, consciously decide to make it the EASIEST mile - drop the shoulders, long exhales, effort easier, pace unchanged. That skill is exactly what you'll use at km 30.
tips.apply: Use the 3-4 word test on every steady/threshold day. Practice the 'easiest mile' trick on the third rep of every session.

tips.title: The secret finisher: 15s on / 15s off
tips.insight: After a tempo + 2-3 min recovery: 15 seconds hard, stand 15 seconds, repeat for 5 minutes (build to 7.5-10). It depletes the ATP system, keeps real speed in the legs, and 'all races are won by being the quickest'.
tips.apply: Bolted onto your Build-phase threshold days. It costs 5 minutes and keeps your top gear alive through marathon training.

tips.title: Training is the non-negotiable; recovery scaffolds around it
tips.insight: A week isn't mileage + sessions. It's: 5-min pre-run activation (calf raises, lunges, crab walks) before EVERY run, post-run stretch/roll, gym 2-3x ('you're not cutting training because your calves get tired - you're adding a calf routine so they don't'), planned meals, hydration, sleep routine, and getting up 20-30 min earlier so sessions aren't rushed - 'give the session the respect it deserves'.
tips.apply: Your day modals now include the activation. With your job: prep breakfast the night before quality days, and treat the Sunday review as part of training.

tips.title: The weekly review: write the zero
tips.insight: 'If you didn't do gym, you have to write zero. You have to make it real.' His weekly review scores the week honestly against what a full week looks like - that acknowledgment is what changes next week. He also swears by goal journaling: 'Are you moving towards your goal or away from it?' - he credits it with making the Olympics.
tips.apply: That's exactly our weekly ritual: the app counts your km, the review names what's missing, and next week responds. No judgment - just no pretending.

tips.title: The day before does the carb loading
tips.insight: Glycogen stores take up to 2 days to fully refill — the pre-long-run dinner alone is too late. Before a big session or race: carb-focused meals mid-afternoon (~15:00) AND evening (~18:00) the day before. Keep it simple and digestible: clean proteins, white rice, food the stomach already knows.
tips.apply: Friday and Saturday are the meals that decide Sunday's long run. Two carb meals Saturday (afternoon + evening), nothing exotic, then the normal morning routine.

tips.title: Any run over ~1h40 MUST be fueled — and race morning is a script
tips.insight: Past ~100 minutes you are out of stored high-intensity fuel, so fueling on runs over 1h40 is mandatory, not optional. Race morning: breakfast 2 hours out, then only water + salt (no sugary drinks), then start nibbling ~10 minutes before the gun and keep nibbling through the warm-up and the whole race.
tips.apply: Your long runs are at or past this line already. Rehearse the exact race script on Sundays: breakfast −2h, water+salt, nibble from −10min. Same brands, same timing, every time.

tips.title: The recovery ladder: walk → jog → 3×1 mile → training
tips.insight: After a marathon (or any brutal race) the cost is muscle damage — micro-tears from the buildup plus race day. First days: walking or easy cycling for blood flow, no hero runs. The test is simple: you can progress when a 15-20 min jog causes no pain DURING and no soreness AFTER. Then the checkpoint back to training: 3×1 mile starting slower than marathon pace, then at it, then slightly faster — comfortable, or you're not ready.
tips.apply: After the race (and after the test half-marathon), follow the ladder — don't jump back into the plan by the calendar, jump back by the pain-free test.

tips.title: After the race, the gym switches your muscles back on
tips.insight: Racing breaks muscle down, and broken-down muscle is WEAK muscle. The one piece of advice Mo Farah gave him after his 61:08 half: get back in the gym within days. 10-14 days post-race: squats, step-ups, small home exercises — re-engage and re-activate what the race switched off.
tips.apply: Your Wed/Fri/Sat gym days aren't just injury-proofing the build — they're also the recovery protocol after the test half and after race day itself.

tips.title: Don't train like a boxer
tips.insight: Most runners do a buildup, race, switch off, then start the next buildup from the exact same starting place — five years later their 10k is identical. The fitness between blocks is what decides the next marathon: if the 10k you'd run 10 weeks out improves from block to block, the marathon outcome improves with it.
tips.apply: After April 2027 the plan isn't 'done' — the off-season goal is a faster 10k, so the next buildup starts from a higher floor. The checkpoint banner exists for exactly this.

tips.title: Shoes are worth seconds — basics are worth minutes
tips.insight: On the super-shoe debate: 'there is much better things you could put your time and energy into that could find you 10 seconds a mile, 15 seconds a mile' — good training, good nutrition and good sleep. Shoes matter on race day; obsessing over them in training is misplaced energy.
tips.apply: Racing shoes for the race and the dress rehearsals. The rest of the budget — attention, money, energy — goes to sleep, food and showing up 4×/week.

tips.title: Plan the next goal before the emptiness hits
tips.insight: The post-marathon low usually isn't about the result — it's losing the direction that got you up every Sunday for 4 months. He recommends deciding, in the month after the race, what the next target is (even a 5k PB) and starting to chip at it. The chipping-away is where the contentment actually lives.
tips.apply: Book something for May-June 2027 before you toe the line in April. Even a local 10k. The plan after the plan.

tips.title: Measure extraction, not times
tips.insight: He calls his 2:09 '97-98% of what I was physically capable of in life ever'. Someone else's 2:28 could be his 2:09; someone's 3:01 might be a 100% extraction. Never compare raw times — compare how much of YOUR potential, given YOUR hand in life (job, family, genetics), you extracted.
tips.apply: 3:30 with a full-time job and 4 runs a week would be a huge extraction. Judge the block by what you got out of yourself, not by what a stranger ran.

tips.title: Discipline beats motivation
tips.insight: Motivation is weather — it comes and goes mid-block. What separates people who arrive at the start line fit is discipline: the run happens because the plan says so, especially on the days nobody's watching and nobody would know if you skipped it.
tips.apply: The 4 runs a week are non-negotiable appointments. On a flat day, downgrade the intensity, never the attendance.

tips.title: 'Just Another Sunday' — race-day confidence is rehearsed
tips.insight: His race-day philosophy: make the marathon feel like just another Sunday. Same breakfast, same fueling script, same warm-up, same controlled first kilometres you've done twenty times. Confidence doesn't come from hype — it comes from race day containing nothing new.
tips.apply: Every Sunday long run in the Specific phase is a rehearsal of the same script. By April, race morning should feel almost boring — that's the goal.
